title: Is k-Clique fixed-parameter tractable, equivalently FPT=W[1]?
formal: Do there exist a total computable function f:ℕ→ℕ, a constant c, and one deterministic algorithm that decides whether an n-vertex graph contains a k-clique in time at most f(k)(n+2)ᶜ on every input? Equivalently, is FPT=W[1]?
definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph G on [n], encoded by its adjacency matrix, and an integer k with 0≤k≤n, encoded in binary. A k-clique is a set of k distinct vertices for which every pair is an edge; k=0 is a yes-instance. Inputs with k>n are rejected immediately, and other malformed inputs are rejected. The parameter is k, not treewidth, degree, or the size of a supplied decomposition. Running time counts deterministic Turing-machine steps on the full input. Constants and the function f may be arbitrary but must be fixed independently of n; the exponent c must also be independent of k. FPT comprises parameterized decision problems solvable in f(k)Nᶜ time, where N is their input encoding length. One equivalent definition of W[1] is the class of parameterized problems reducible to k-Clique by a deterministic f(k)Nᶜ-time many-one reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of k alone. This is the standard parameterized reduction convention under which Clique is W[1]-complete. No randomness, advice, or promise about G is allowed.
answer_criterion: Answer yes with such an algorithm for some computable f and fixed c. Answer no by proving that every deterministic exact Clique algorithm fails to satisfy every bound of this form. Proving a lower bound only under ETH or FPT≠W[1] does not resolve the class separation; finding an n^{g(k)} algorithm with unbounded g does not establish membership in FPT.
context:
For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, 2^{2^k}n³ meets the requested form, while n^{k/10} does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If P=NP then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus FPT≠W[1] is a stronger separation conjecture than P≠NP in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every W[1] problem in FPT time. This is why a W[1]-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out f(k)n^{o(k)} algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is W[1]-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove FPT≠W[1].
why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: Downey and Fellows develop the W-hierarchy and the completeness framework that makes parameterized Clique a canonical target for the FPT-versus-W[1] question.
ETH-based reductions establish the stronger conditional obstruction to f(k)n^{o(k)} Clique algorithms; the textbook develops this in its parameterized lower-bound chapters.
Bottesch studies structural and relativization evidence concerning FPT and W[1], explicitly distinguishing this conjecture from P≠NP. No unrelativized separation is proved.
Lin proves constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique W[1]-hard, transferring the same central assumption to approximate search.
Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit, and Liu give a simpler combinatorial construction for the k^{o(1)} parameterized Clique inapproximability bound.
Abboud, Fischer, and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique running times by logarithmic factors. The Algorithmica publication of 22 May 2026 retains dependence on k in the exponent of n.

title: Does the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis hold?
formal: For every real ε∈(0,1), does there exist an integer k≥3 such that no deterministic algorithm decides k-SAT on n variables and input length L in time $O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}L^c)$ for any fixed constant c? Here k is fixed independently of n and L. This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).
definitions: A k-SAT input is an explicitly encoded conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most k literals xᵢ or ¬xᵢ. Variables are relabeled consecutively and n counts the distinct variables actually present; L counts the full binary formula encoding, including literal indices and delimiters. The decision is exact satisfiability, with no promise about clause density, the number of satisfying assignments, or how the formula was generated. Empty clauses make the input unsatisfiable, and the empty conjunction is satisfiable. Running time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine time. For a fixed k, the algorithm, polynomial exponent, and hidden constant may depend on k and ε, but not on the individual formula. Define sₖ=inf{α≥0 : k-SAT has an O(2^{αn}Lᶜ)-time deterministic algorithm for some constant c}. SETH equivalently asserts limₖ→∞sₖ=1; monotonicity follows because k-SAT is a restriction of (k+1)-SAT. Polynomial factors are retained explicitly so reading the input is allowed even when clauses are repeated. No advice, oracle, random bits, or quantum computation is allowed.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated exclusion for every ε>0, or refute it by finding one fixed ε>0 such that every fixed width k has a deterministic O(2^{(1−ε)n}L^{c_k})-time algorithm. The algorithms may depend on k; the exponential saving ε must not. An improvement for only one width, or savings that tend to zero as k grows, do not refute SETH.
context:
Exhaustive search tries all 2ⁿ assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially 2ⁿ time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A 2^{0.9n}-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds 2^{(1−1/k)n} would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond P≠NP, which by itself allows intermediate running times such as 2^{√n}.

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Recent work continues to sharpen small-width algorithms. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports a slightly improved randomized PPSZ bound for general 3-SAT, distinguished from its better bound under a unique-solution promise. Both the fixed width and use of randomness keep this improvement outside the deterministic, all-width saving required to refute the present statement.
why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

importance.reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates for k-SAT and their growth with clause width, using critical clauses and sparsification.
SETH-based reductions extend to numerous problems in polynomial time. Vassilevska Williams surveys the reductions, hypotheses, and resulting equivalence and hardness questions.
The parameterized-algorithms textbook gives explicit deterministic definitions of ETH and SETH and separately discusses their randomized analogues.

Jiang and Cai report randomized O*(1.307031578ⁿ) time for general 3-SAT and O*(1.306969598ⁿ) for Unique-3-SAT by refining the analysis of PPSZ. These are preprint bounds for fixed width, not a constant saving valid for every k.
